prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Plan comparison (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Feature" · longest unbreakable word 56px · one-line width 83px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 79px · one-line width 79px
  col 3: header "Pro" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 4: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 229px
  col 5: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 419px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

These are all candidate designs you produced, rendered in a real browser:
Design r1B: widths [104, 100, 87, 105, 220] · table 617×358px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 83, 36, 83] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 257px
Design r1C: widths [78, 101, 88, 97, 96] · table 461×707px · row heights [36, 153, 153, 176, 60, 129] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 7 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 101px
Design r2A: widths [80, 100, 87, 108, 133] · table 509×544px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 129, 60, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 5 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 149px
Design r2B: widths [78, 100, 87, 96, 119] · table 481×614px · row heights [36, 129, 129, 153, 60, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 6 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 121px
Design r2C: widths [96, 100, 87, 108, 140] · table 532×498px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 106, 36, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 172px
Design r3A: widths [77, 100, 87, 96, 140] · table 501×521px · row heights [36, 106, 106, 106, 60, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 141px
Design r3B: widths [77, 100, 87, 96, 160] · table 521×474px · row heights [36, 83, 83, 106, 60, 106] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 161px
Design r3C: widths [77, 100, 87, 96, 94] · table 455×730px · row heights [36, 153, 153, 176, 60, 153] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 7 lines · mid-word splits 0 · OVERFLOWS the box by 95px

Decide as a designer:
- "preferred": the best design(s). Name more than one only if they are genuinely equally good.
- "acceptable": other designs a careful designer would still publish.
- "bad": designs with clear visual faults, each with the fault. If none of these is clearly bad, also return ONE deliberately bad but plausible alternative as "contrast" widths and say what is wrong with it.
- "ranges": for each column, the px range within which the preferred design stays equally good (keep other columns' proportions).
- "rationale": 2–4 concrete sentences about this table.
- "principles": observations that seem GENERAL (likely to hold for other tables) vs SPECIFIC to this case.
- "tradeoffs" and "uncertain": what reasonable designers could disagree on.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"preferred":["name"],"acceptable":["name"],"bad":[{"design":"name","why":""}],"contrast":{"widths":[int px],"why":""} or null,"ranges":[[min,max]],"rationale":"","principles":{"general":[""],"specific":[""]},"tradeoffs":"","uncertain":""}

log.raw: {"preferred":["r3B"],"acceptable":["r2C","r3A","r1B"],"bad":[{"design":"r1C","why":"Squeezes every column, including Notes down to 75px of text, so the free-text column collapses into 7-line fragments and the table balloons to 707px tall; rows 153–176px high destroy the vertical rhythm that makes a comparison table scannable, and 'Feature'/'Audit log' also wrap."},{"design":"r3C","why":"Same failure in the extreme: Notes at 73px of text (7 lines, 730px table), plus a 1px-under-budget total that gains nothing — the narrowest table of the set is also the tallest, so the squeeze buys no legibility anywhere."},{"design":"r2A","why":"Worst of both worlds: the four plan columns still exceed the box (Enterprise clipped mid-header at 87px of text) while Notes at 112px of text still runs to 5 lines and 106–129px rows — it neither keeps the comparison in view nor makes the notes readable."},{"design":"r2B","why":"Notes at 98px of text gives 6-line cells and 129–153px rows, and Enterprise is again cut off at the box edge; the table is 614px tall and still scrolls 121px, paying both costs without collecting either benefit."}],"contrast":null,"ranges":[[77,96],[100,112],[87,96],[96,110],[150,220]],"rationale":"Every candidate overflows 360px, so the real decision is where the cut falls: r3B places the four comparison columns (77+100+87+96 = 360) exactly inside the box, so the reader can compare plans without scrolling and only the supplementary Notes column is pushed off-screen. Because Notes then gets 139px of text, rows stay at 83–106px and the whole table is 474px tall — the compact version of the same content. The Feature column at 77px breaks 'SSO / SAML' at its slash rather than mid-word, costing one extra line in one row, which is a fair trade for keeping Enterprise fully visible. Designs that clip Enterprise mid-header (r1B, r2A, r2B, r2C) break the very comparison the table exists for; designs that starve Notes (r1C, r3C) turn prose into seven-line fragments.","principles":{"general":["In a horizontally scrolling table, spend the scroll on the free-text/notes column, not on the columns the reader must compare side by side — a clipped comparison column breaks the table's core task, a clipped notes column merely defers it.","Give a prose column enough width to break at clause boundaries; below roughly 15–20 characters per line every cell becomes a fragment stack and row height explodes, which is worse than horizontal scrolling.","Columns playing the same role (Free/Pro/Enterprise) should be near-equal and sized to their longest token; the row-label and notes columns are different roles and deserve visibly different widths. Symmetry here would be a fault.","A row-label column may be narrower than its widest phrase if the break falls on a natural separator (space, slash) — a one-line cost in one row is cheaper than 20px stolen from every other column."],"specific":["The four plan columns need 387px at their natural one-line minimum (83+79+66+75 plus 84px padding), just over the 360px box, so some clipping or squeezing is unavoidable; the only free variable is how much overflow to accept and where.","The Notes column's one-line width is 419px, so it can never be one-line at any viable total — it is structurally the designated scroll target and should be sized for readability, not for fitting.","'Enterprise' at exactly 75px of available text in r3B has zero slack; a different font stack or subpixel rounding could wrap it, which argues for a few px of headroom if the budget allows."]},"tradeoffs":"r1B is the honest rival: its rows are the shortest (358px table, 3-line maximum) and its Notes column at 199px reads as real sentences, which is the best notes legibility of the set — but it pays with 257px of scroll and clips 'Enterprise' mid-word, so the comparison only works after scrolling. A designer who treats Notes as primary content and the plans as a header row could legitimately choose it; one who treats the plan comparison as the table's job must choose r3B or r2C.","uncertain":"Whether the 1px overshoot (360 vs the 359 budget) in r3B/r3A is acceptable, and whether the Notes column should exist at all at this width — dropping it, or moving it to a second line spanning under each row, may be a better answer than any width assignment. I am also not certain how much the exact 75px fit of 'Enterprise' depends on rendering."}
